title: Ai2 Finds Minor Prompt Changes Shift AI Novelty Rating Accuracy by More Than 50 Points
summary:
Frontier large language models often struggle to provide consistent ratings when evaluating the originality of scientific research. A study by the Allen Institute for AI found that modifying the phrasing of a prompt can lead to wildly different outcomes; in one test, GPT-5.4 identified a human-generated research idea as novel 93.5% of the time when asked which idea reviewers had judged as such, but the rate fell to 40.9% when asked simply which idea was novel. Across various tests, these prompt adjustments shifted accuracy by more than 50 points in some cases.

The researchers used a benchmark based on reviewer comments from ICLR 2026 and found that higher intelligence and more complex toolsets did not necessarily lead to better judgments. A simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 achieved a 0.89 macro-F1 score, outperforming a GPT-5.6 Sol agent with iterative literature search that scored 0.78 despite being roughly 10 times more expensive per judgment. Ai2 has open-sourced the benchmark data and code to allow other models to be tested as judges.

selectedTweets.text:
Uh oh. If your AI benchmark uses an LLM-as-judge, you might want to read this.

AllenAI tested six frontier models to see whether research ideas were actually novel.

And tiny changes to the judge prompt caused crazy swings.

GPT-5.4, same basic idea pairs
“Which was judged novel?” → 93.5%
“Which is novel?” → 40.9%
“Which was judged more novel?” → 59.7%

Across the study, changing the prompt moved accuracy by 👉50+ points 👈 in some cases and occasionally pushed judges below chance.

So naturally they tried giving the judge more intelligence and tools.

Didn't fix it.

A GPT-5.6 Sol agent running xhigh reasoning with iterative literature search and no search cap scored
→ 0.78 macro-F1

Claude Opus 4.6 with only 5 pre-retrieved abstracts did about 
→ 0.89

And the big agentic setup cost ~10× more per judgment.

Two purpose-built novelty-evaluation systems lost to the researchers' cheapest simple prompted judge by
→ 8–29 macro-F1 points

while costing up to
→ 32× MORE

🎯 Lesson Learned 👉 More model, more reasoning more RAG, and more money, doesn't automatically mean a better judge.

AllenAI open-sourced the benchmark + code too, so now I want to see Qwen, DeepSeek and other local models run as the judges.

The safer benchmark recipe is
👨‍🔬 build a human-rated calibration set
🤖 test the LLM judge against it
🔄 test multiple prompt/order variations
🗳️ aggregate multiple judgments
👀 send close calls back to humans
